passage: On the bus home in Stockholm, Ingrid was telling Rafael about her future again. "I'm going to be a surgeon. Heart surgery, like in that documentary. I'll work in a big hospital, maybe travel to places that need doctors." Rafael nodded. "Cool. So what are you doing for it this month?" Ingrid opened her mouth. "Well... I mean, I'll study." "Study what, though? You said you hate chemistry." "I'll get to it." She looked out of the window. Her biology test was in two weeks. She hadn't opened the chapter. The dream felt so bright and so far away that there was nothing to do about it today.

qa.q: What kind of surgeon does Ingrid want to be?
qa.a: A heart surgeon, like in that documentary.

qa.q: Why did Ingrid feel there was nothing to do about her dream today?
qa.a: Ingrid felt excited about the dream but lost about how to start, since it was so bright and far away that it pointed to no action now.

qa.q: What nearer step could Ingrid set for this month?
qa.a: She could study the biology chapter a little each day before the test in two weeks, and ask a teacher for help with chemistry.

qa.q: Why might Rafael ask about this month rather than the dream?
qa.a: Rafael seems to sense the dream has no path yet, and gently asks the question that could turn it into a first step.

grounding: A teenager in Sweden dreams of being a surgeon but has no plan for the coming weeks.

passage: In the school counsellor's room, Sonali said it with total confidence: "Doctor. Paediatrician. I've wanted it since I was six." Saurabh sir smiled and pulled out a sheet. "Wonderful. What's your plan for this month?" Sonali blinked. "This month? I'll... prepare for the entrance exam. Eventually." "Which subjects are strongest right now?" "Biology. Physics is... not great. I got 14 out of 40." "Have you looked at the entrance syllabus?" She shook her head. She had pictured the white coat a hundred times, the children's ward, the grateful parents. She had never pictured this month. Saurabh sir tapped the sheet. "Let's break it down. Start with physics, just one chapter by the 30th." Sonali stared at the blank lines, feeling both deflated and oddly relieved.

qa.q: What did Sonali get in physics?
Why did Sonali feel both deflated and oddly relieved?
qa.a: The bright dream suddenly looked like a lot of work, but having one clear chapter to start with made it feel reachable.

qa.q: What does Saurabh sir's 'one chapter by the 30th' offer that the dream alone didn't?
qa.a: A near, specific step Sonali can act on this month, which turns a far-off goal into daily direction.

qa.q: How might Saurabh sir see students who arrive with big dreams but no plan?
qa.a: He seems to welcome the dream but knows it needs nearer steps, so he helps break it down without dismissing it.

grounding: A teenager sure she will be a doctor discovers in a counselling session that she has no plan for this month.

passage:
Dear Pallavi didi,
You won't believe it, I've decided I'm going to be a doctor like you! I've already told everyone at school. I even practised writing "Dr Himani" in my rough book. 😊
Okay, but here's a problem. Mummy asked me yesterday what I'm doing to get there, and I said, "Studying," and she said, "Which chapter, today?" And I didn't know. I have a science test on the 20th and I haven't started. I keep thinking about the hospital and the stethoscope, but I don't know what to do on a normal Tuesday.
How did you do it when you were my age? Did you have a plan for every month, or did you just want it very badly?
Please write back soon.
Love,
Himani

qa.q: When is Himani's science test?
What is worrying Himani about the dream?
qa.a: Himani loves imagining the hospital and stethoscope, but worries about not knowing what to do on a normal Tuesday to get there.

qa.q: What could Pallavi didi suggest Himani do this month?
qa.a: She could suggest starting the science chapter for the 20th, a little each day, so the far-off goal becomes a daily step.

qa.q: Why might Mummy have asked 'Which chapter, today?'
qa.a: Mummy seems to want the big dream to turn into daily action, and her question points Himani to the very next step.

grounding: In a letter, a young teenager dreams of becoming a doctor but has no idea what to do this month.

passage:
Rehana, I've decided. I'm going to be a doctor. A heart doctor, in a big hospital, with my own cabin and a name board: Dr Jyoti Rawat. I can already see it.
What am I doing this month for it? Uh... studying? Like, generally.
No, I haven't looked at which entrance exam. That's in Class 12, na, years away. Biology marks? 58 last term. But that's just Class 10, it doesn't count.
Why are you making that face?
Okay, fine. What would a future heart doctor be doing in Class 10, in October? Maybe getting my biology up? Finding out what the exam even is? Asking Rukhsana's cousin, who's in medical college, how she started?
Hmm. That's actually a list. Write it down before I forget. Three things for this month. The name board can wait.

qa.q: What were Jyoti's biology marks last term?
Why does the doctor dream feel so real to Jyoti even without a plan?
qa.a: Jyoti can picture the cabin and name board vividly; the far-off image is inspiring, so having no step for this month doesn't feel like a problem at first.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Rehana's face made Jyoti ask what a future heart doctor would do this October; that produced three near steps: raise biology marks, learn about the exam and talk to the cousin in medical college.

qa.q: What might Rehana have been thinking when making 'that face'?
qa.a: Rehana probably doubted that 'studying, generally' would lead to a name board, and wanted Jyoti to notice the missing plan without saying it outright.

grounding: A teenager dreams vividly of becoming a doctor but has no plan for the month, until a friend's look prompts three near steps.

passage:
I'm Vikas, Sunaina's younger brother. Sunaina is going to be a doctor. Everyone in our building knows, because she tells them. The toy stethoscope she got at six still hangs on her cupboard, and there's a poster of the human heart above her bed.
But here's what I see. Her biology notebook has been at the bottom of her bag since the holidays. When Papa asked which exam she needs to take, she said, 'The medical one,' and changed the subject. In the evenings she watches hospital shows and says, 'That'll be me.'
Last week her friend Gayatri asked what she was doing this month to get there. Sunaina went quiet for a long time.
I don't know what she was thinking. Maybe she was scared. Maybe she'd just never thought about it. Afterwards, though, she took out the biology notebook.

qa.q: What hangs on Sunaina's cupboard?
qa.a: The toy stethoscope she got at six.

qa.q: What might Sunaina's long silence after Gayatri's question suggest?
qa.a: It may suggest she realised she had no plan for the month; the dream was vivid, but the near steps were missing, and that may have worried her.

qa.q: What choice after Gayatri's question could start to close the gap, and why?
qa.a: Taking out the biology notebook; one concrete step this month, like a weekly biology target, links the far goal to everyday action.

qa.q: How does Vikas see the gap between Sunaina's dream and her days?
qa.a: Vikas notices the posters and the talk but also the buried notebook and vague answers, and is unsure whether she is scared or has simply never thought about the steps.

grounding: A younger brother observes a teenager who talks constantly about becoming a doctor but has no near-term plan, until a friend's question stops her.
